cells.tense: The knowing is here at the bench, and the pen is steady in the hand.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Take an ending you didn't choose, set down what it gave you that you'd keep, and stop the count at that column.
cells.core:
Your sense of what's fair lives close to the hands, and it does its best work with what's actually there. A finished stretch gets counted honestly — some of it spent, some held — and the count comes out clean enough to stand on. You can tell when something is done. That's what lets the next thing start without you dragging the old one along.

When you can, count one ending for yourself: what it gave you, what was lost, what you're keeping. Not for anyone else. The fair move isn't a clean slate — it's an accurate one. Fairness checked against the real goods moves by itself, because the account closes without you pushing.

Rest goes back to what it wasn't sure it was owed.

cells.tense: You're running the account forward into times that haven't happened yet.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: This week, take on a piece of help that ends — a form, a shift, a ride — finish it clean, and don't audit the return.
cells.core:
The fair thing hasn't happened yet and you've already settled it — what you'll owe, what you'll be owed, where the accounting lands. The sums are private and constant, and they leave you braced against a room you're not standing in. Fairness borrowed from tomorrow can't be balanced today.

There's an easier way to walk into a room than pre-clearing the debt. This week, take one concrete piece of help to one person and finish it clean — no follow-up tally, no waiting to see what comes back. The strength goes outward where it's needed, and the run-ahead quiets into the room you're in.

Done is the whole point of it.

cells.tense: You crossed the threshold already and your weight is still behind it.
cells.act: point to the passage you can see
cells.ask: For someone stuck, mark the next step you can see for them — one line, sent once, nothing after it.
cells.core:
The finishing door is behind you, and you haven't come all the way through it. The work got done — you can look at it — but some part of you is still tied to whether it counted, and that tie holds the door open. It's hard to name what feels fair when you can't tell if the thing that closed was actually closed.

There's a way back that isn't more weighing. For someone else, put down in one line the next step you can see for them, sent once, with nothing after it. You can only describe a route from further along it. The door shuts the next time your feet are past it.

The account settles after you stop checking it.

cells.tense: Your hand is on the pen, and you'd tell the room it writes itself.
cells.act: sort the kinds of pull from one another
cells.ask: Notice the pulls on you right now. Sort them into what's yours and what isn't, and act from the first pile only.
cells.core:
The line you draw on what's fair keeps getting drawn before you look at it, and you'd say that's just how the room is. It arrives as a fact about a situation — this owes that, this is owed nothing — and somewhere behind it your own sense is doing the measuring. The moral tone in a room tends to match your read of it. People can act on that clarity faster than they can say where it came from.

There is a simple fix for work you can't see yourself doing. Notice the pulls on you at this moment — the loyalty, the leftover obligation, the thing you're still counting for someone else. Sort them into what's yours. The rest were not on your account, and they leave when you stop holding them.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person keeps a private ledger of what's owed — the record says the felt-sense of fairness is active, not that they tally. The reader could reasonably say 'I don't keep score, I just know when something's off.' The asks survive being wrong because each one is a doable act (counting what an ending gave, giving help once, walking someone through a route, sorting pulls) that teaches something regardless of whether 'Conscience' is the right read. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything that implies they are morally anxious by nature; the cells are written so the person can say 'no, that's not what's happening' and still have something to use.
